qs.q: A 25-year-old man presents with progressive muscle weakness and is found to have a mutation in the dystrophin gene. Which best explains why this mutation leads to sarcolemmal fragility?
o: Depletion of glycogen phosphorylase activity in skeletal myofibrils
Disruption of high-flux calcium binding sites inside the reticulum
Inhibition of myosin heavy chain phosphorylation during contraction
Impairment of acetylcholine receptor clustering at the motor endplate
Loss of anchoring between intracellular actin and extracellular matrix
qs.e: Dystrophin links the intracellular actin cytoskeleton to the extracellular matrix, protecting membranes from contraction-induced stress.

qs.q: A 25-year-old man presents with progressive muscle weakness. Genetic testing reveals a mutation in the dystrophin gene. Which best explains why this mutation leads to muscle fiber damage during contraction?
o: Excessive intracellular calcium sequestration by reticulum
Defective oxidative phosphorylation in mitochondrial cells
Impaired neurotransmitter release at neuromuscular junctions
Abnormal collagen deposition within endomysial spaces
Loss of sarcolemma mechanical stability during contraction
qs.e: Dystrophin links the intracellular cytoskeleton to extracellular matrix, protecting membranes from contraction-induced injury.

qs.q: A 5-year-old boy presents with progressive muscle weakness and is diagnosed with Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy (DMD). Which type of mutation in the dystrophin gene is responsible for this condition?
qs.e: Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy is caused by a nonsense mutation that introduces a premature stop codon, leading to a truncated protein. A silent mutation would not alter the phenotype or cause such a severe condition.
